why: Outside sounds can warn you of danger before you see it.

items.q: Why should you keep your music volume low while driving?
choices: So you can hear sirens and horns outside
Because loud music is always illegal

items.q: You should be able to hear emergency sirens over your car stereo.

fact: In Idaho, reading, writing, or sending text messages while driving is illegal and is an infraction. Hands-free use with neither hand is not covered by this law.
why: Texting takes your eyes, hands, and mind off driving.

items.q: In Idaho, reading a text message while driving is legal as long as you do not reply.
Which is allowed under Idaho's texting law while driving?
choices: Using a hands-free device without either hand
Reading a text at a stop sign
Typing a short reply on a straight road
Sending a text with one hand on the wheel

items.q: In Idaho, what kind of offense is texting while driving?

fact: A texting-while-driving conviction brings a fine but no points on your driving record. It counts as a moving violation only when driving a commercial motor vehicle.
why: The law sets the penalty as a fine for regular drivers, with stricter treatment for commercial drivers.

items.q: For a regular (non-commercial) driver in Idaho, what does a texting-while-driving conviction bring?
choices: A fine, with no points on the record
Points on the record and a fine

items.q: A texting-while-driving conviction adds points to a regular Idaho driver's record.

fact: Stop driving when you feel drowsy. Pull off at the first rest stop or service area and take a nap. Do not rely on stay-awake drugs or energy drinks.
why: Drowsiness is one of the greatest killers on interstate highways, and stimulants can make driving even more dangerous.

items.q: You are on the interstate and start to feel very sleepy. What should you do?
choices: Get off at the first rest stop and take a nap
Drink an energy drink and keep going
Open the window and turn up the music
Drive faster to get there sooner

items.q: Energy drinks are a safe way to stay alert when you are drowsy while driving.

fact: Highway hypnosis is drowsiness caused by monotony and the steady sound of wind and tires. Prevent it by shifting your eyes often to objects near and far, left and right.
why: Moving your eyes keeps your brain active on long, boring stretches of road.

items.q: What is highway hypnosis?
choices: Drowsiness caused by monotony and road noise

items.q: How can you help prevent highway hypnosis?
choices: Keep shifting your eyes to objects near and far

fact: Texting while driving is six times more dangerous than driving impaired. If you must use a phone, park in a safe place first.
why: Texting takes your eyes and attention off the road for long stretches.

items.q: Texting while driving is how many times more dangerous than driving impaired?
You need to answer an important text while driving on a busy road. What should you do?
choices: Park in a safe place first, then reply
Reply quickly at the next red light
Hold the phone low and type fast
Slow down and type with one hand

fact: Alive at 25 is a defensive driving course for people 15 through 24 years old, taught by law enforcement.
why: Young drivers are over-represented in crash statistics.

items.q: Who is the Alive at 25 course for?
Alive at 25 is a defensive driving course presented by law enforcement.

fact: When law enforcement stops you, stay calm, use your turn signal, and pull to the side of the road as soon as it is safe. Turn off the engine and radio, stay in the vehicle unless told to get out, and keep your hands on the steering wheel.
why: Visible hands and calm actions help both you and the officer feel safe.

items.q: An officer pulls you over and walks toward your car. Where should your hands be?
choices: In your lap out of sight

items.q: When pulled over, you should get out of your car and walk to the officer.

fact: During a stop, do not search for your license or papers until the officer asks. If they are out of reach, tell the officer where they are before reaching. If you have a weapon in the vehicle, tell the officer at first contact.
why: Sudden reaching can look like a threat, so telling the officer first keeps everyone safe.

items.q: The officer asks for your registration, which is in the glove box. What should you do first?
choices: Tell the officer where it is before reaching
Get out and get it from the trunk

items.q: If you have a weapon in your vehicle, you should tell the officer when they first contact you.

fact: Signing a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt, but refusing to sign it may lead to your arrest. You can contest the ticket in court.
why: Your signature only shows you received the ticket; the court decides guilt.

items.q: Signing a traffic ticket means you admit you are guilty.
What may happen if you refuse to sign a traffic ticket?

fact: A slow moving vehicle sign is an orange triangle with red edges. It is mostly used on farm and construction equipment. Slow down and approach the vehicle with caution.
why: These vehicles travel much slower than normal traffic, so you can close the gap very quickly.
hook: Orange triangle with red edges = slow vehicle ahead.

items.q: Where is the slow moving vehicle sign mostly used?
On a rural road you see an orange triangle with red borders on the back of a tractor ahead. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and approach with caution
Keep your speed; it will pull over
Follow closely so you can pass quickly

fact: A SHARE THE ROAD sign is placed under a bicycle sign on roads without bike lanes. It warns drivers and bicyclists to share the road, often where lanes or shoulders are narrow or traffic is heavy or fast.
why: Without a bike lane, cars and bikes must use the same space.
signDesc: Yellow rectangular plaque with black text SHARE THE ROAD, mounted below a yellow diamond bicycle sign

items.q: What does this sign mean?
choices: Drivers and bicyclists must share the roadway
Bike lane ahead for bikes only

items.q: Where is a SHARE THE ROAD sign used?
choices: Only on roads with bike lanes

items.q: A Share the Road sign is used on roads that already have bike lanes.

fact: A solid white line with a bicycle symbol marks a bike lane for bicycles only. Bicycles in it must travel in the same direction as the traffic next to it.
why: Riding with traffic makes bicyclists predictable to drivers.

items.q: Which way must bicycles travel in a marked bike lane?
choices: The same direction as nearby traffic
Against traffic so they can see cars
Only the direction of the arrow on the sign

items.q: Cars may drive in a lane marked with a solid white line and bicycle symbol.

fact: Some buses and trucks must stop at every railroad crossing, so be ready to stop when following them.
why: If you do not expect their stop, you could rear-end them.

items.q: You are following a school bus toward a railroad crossing with no train coming. What should you expect?
choices: The bus may stop at the crossing
The bus will speed up to cross
The bus will pull onto the shoulder to let you pass
The bus will only slow down

items.q: Some buses and trucks are required to stop at all railroad crossings.

fact: You do not have to stop for a school bus going the opposite direction on a highway with four or more lanes, with two lanes going each way.
why: On a road with two lanes going each way, you are far from the side of the road where children get on and off the bus.

items.q: You are on a highway with two lanes each way. A school bus on the other side, going the opposite direction, stops with red lights flashing. What do you do?
choices: Continue with care; you do not have to stop
Stop until the lights turn off
Stop only if you see children

items.q: On a highway with at least how many total lanes do drivers going the opposite direction not have to stop for a school bus?
On a two-lane road, drivers going the opposite direction from a stopped school bus with flashing red lights do not need to stop.

fact: You must stop for a school bus that has its red lights flashing or its stop arm out. Stay stopped until the lights stop, and all children are clear of the road and the bus. Never pass a stopped school bus that is loading or unloading.
why: Children may run across the road without looking, often in front of the bus where they are hard to see.

items.q: On a two-lane road, a school bus coming toward you stops and turns on its flashing red lights. What do you do?
choices: Stop and stay stopped until children are clear and the lights stop
Keep going because the bus is in the other lane
Slow to 20 mph and pass carefully
Stop, then go once the stop arm starts to fold

items.q: You may pass a stopped school bus with flashing red lights if you go slowly.

fact: Vehicles built to go no faster than 25 mph may use public highways only in daylight (30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset), with some exceptions for snow removal and farm equipment with flashing lights. They must show the slow-moving vehicle emblem.
why: Very slow vehicles are hard for faster drivers to judge, especially in the dark.

items.q: Slow-moving vehicles are those designed to travel no faster than how many mph?
Slow-moving vehicles may start using the highway how many minutes before sunrise?
A neighbor wants to drive a vehicle built for a top speed of 20 mph on a public highway. It is not snow-removal or farm equipment. When may it be driven there?
choices: Only from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset
Any time if it has headlights
Only at night when traffic is light

fact: Children darting out from between parked cars is a common cause of serious injury. Use extra caution near parked cars and when backing out of a driveway.
why: Children are often too short to be seen near parked cars, and an unseen playmate may follow.

items.q: You see a ball roll into the street from between parked cars. What should you expect?
choices: A child may run out after it
Nothing; it is just a ball
The ball will stop on its own
A parked car will start moving

items.q: When you see a child near the road, there may be another child nearby whom you cannot see.

fact: When a pedestrian is hit, the chance of death rises sharply as vehicle speed increases. Slow down and watch carefully for pedestrians, especially at night or in rain, snow, fog, or glare.
why: Lower speed gives you more time to stop and causes less harm if you do hit someone.

items.q: What happens to pedestrian deaths as vehicle speed increases?
It is easier to see pedestrians entering the street in fog or sun glare.

fact: A bicyclist may move away from the right edge when passing, turning left, avoiding an obstacle, or when the lane is too narrow for a bike and a car side by side.
why: In these cases, riding at the edge would be unsafe for the bicyclist.

items.q: When may a bicyclist ride away from the right edge of the road?
choices: Whenever they want to go faster
Only when riding in a group

items.q: A bicyclist is riding in the center of a narrow lane where a car cannot safely pass. What should you do?
choices: Stay back patiently and do not follow too closely
Tailgate to show you want to pass

fact: When passing a bicyclist, move into the left lane if you can. If not, leave at least 3 feet of space. Higher speeds need more space.
why: Bicyclists may need room to avoid debris or swerve, and they have little protection.

items.q: What is the minimum space you should leave when passing a bicyclist?
How much space should you leave when passing a bicyclist?
A typical 12-foot travel lane is wide enough to safely share side by side with a bicyclist.

fact: In Idaho, a bicyclist may go through a red light with caution after stopping and yielding to vehicles in or near the intersection. For a right turn on red, they do not need to fully stop but must still yield.
why: Knowing this law helps you expect bicyclists to move at red lights.

items.q: In Idaho, a bicyclist may proceed through a red light after stopping and yielding to vehicles.
What must an Idaho bicyclist do before going straight through a red light?
choices: Stop and yield to vehicles in or near the intersection
Wait for the light to turn green
Only slow down; no stop is needed

fact: Bicyclists may ride on all Idaho roads, have the same rights as drivers, and must ride with the flow of traffic, as far right as is safe.
why: Riding with traffic and near the edge makes bicyclists predictable to drivers.

items.q: Which direction must bicyclists ride on Idaho roads?
Bicyclists in Idaho have the same rights on the road as drivers.

fact: In Idaho, bicyclists do not have to come to a full stop at stop signs, but they must yield to vehicles in or near the intersection and then go with caution.
why: Idaho law treats a stop sign as a yield for bicyclists, so do not be surprised when a cyclist rolls through.

items.q: In Idaho, bicyclists must come to a complete stop at every stop sign.
What must an Idaho bicyclist do at a stop sign?
choices: Yield to vehicles at or near the intersection, then proceed with caution
Come to a full stop and wait 3 seconds
Get off and walk the bike across
Nothing; bicycles may ignore stop signs

fact: When you come up to a person riding a horse, slow down, pass with plenty of room, and never use your horn. If the rider is having trouble controlling the horse, use extreme care and stop if needed.
why: A frightened horse can jump into your path and cause a crash.

items.q: You come up behind a person riding a horse on a rural road. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and pass with plenty of room, without honking
Honk to let the rider know you are there
Flash your lights and pass close

items.q: Horseback riders on public roads have the same rights and must obey the same rules as drivers.

fact: At intersections, scan the corners more than once. A bicyclist can travel 50 to 100 feet in a few seconds.
why: What you saw on your first look may have changed by the time you move.

items.q: About how far can a bicyclist travel in just a few seconds?
At an intersection, one look at the corners is enough because bicyclists move slowly.

fact: If a bicyclist is ahead of you when you plan to turn right, slow down and stay behind them until they pass your turn. Do not try to beat them.
why: Turning across a bicyclist causes a 'right hook' crash.

items.q: You plan to turn right at the next corner, and a bicyclist is riding just ahead of you on the right. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and stay behind the bicyclist until they pass the corner
Speed up and turn in front of the bicyclist
Turn quickly while the bicyclist is still beside you

items.q: What is a 'right hook' crash?
choices: A car turning right across a bicyclist's path
A car hitting a curb on a right turn
A bike turning right into a car
Two cars turning right at once

fact: When stopped and about to turn right, look left, right, and behind you, checking right first. A bicyclist may be coming on your right.
why: A cyclist on the sidewalk, riding against traffic, or pulled up beside you may be on your right.

items.q: You are stopped and want to turn right. Which direction should you check first?
Before turning right from a stop, it is enough to look only to the left.

fact: Never honk when close to a bicyclist. To make sure a bicyclist sees you, wave or nod and wait for their reaction.
why: A horn can startle a bicyclist and cause them to swerve.

items.q: You want to be sure a nearby bicyclist sees you. What should you do?
choices: Wave or nod and wait for a reaction

items.q: Honking close to a bicyclist is a good way to warn them.

fact: After parallel parking, open the driver's door with your far hand (the right hand). This turns your body so you look in the mirror and over your shoulder for bicyclists.
why: The handbook says this habit helps prevent the most common type of crash involving bicyclists: a door opened into a passing rider.

items.q: When getting out after parallel parking, which hand should you use to open the driver's door?
choices: The hand farther from the door
The hand closer to the door
Either hand, if you are quick
Neither; let a passenger open it

items.q: Why should you check for bicyclists before opening your car door on the street side?
choices: It helps prevent the most common type of bicycle crash

fact: Motorcycles are entitled to a full lane. Never drive in the same lane beside a motorcycle, even if the lane is wide.
why: Riders change position in the lane to see, be seen, and avoid objects.

items.q: If a motorcycle is riding far to one side of a wide lane, you may share the lane with it.
How much lane width is a motorcycle entitled to?

fact: Before turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle, look, then look again. Be sure you see the motorcycle and know its speed.
why: Cars turning left in front of motorcycles cause serious crashes because drivers miss or misjudge them.

items.q: You are waiting to turn left and see an oncoming motorcycle. What should you do?
choices: Look again to judge its speed before turning
Assume it is far away because it looks small

items.q: Left turns in front of oncoming motorcycles are a cause of serious crashes.

fact: Motorcyclists have the same rights and duties as other road users. About half of all motorcycle crashes involve another motor vehicle, partly because motorcycles are small, easy to hide in blind spots, and hard to judge for speed and distance.
why: Being hard to see is why drivers often miss motorcycles.

items.q: It can be hard to judge how fast a motorcycle is moving or how far away it is.
About what share of motorcycle crashes involve another motor vehicle?

fact: Most motorcycle turn signals do not turn off by themselves. Before turning in front of a motorcycle with a flashing signal, make sure it is really turning.
why: The rider may have forgotten to cancel the signal and may keep going straight into your path.

items.q: An oncoming motorcycle has its right turn signal on. You want to turn left in front of it. What should you do?
choices: Wait until you are sure it is actually turning
Turn now because it is signaling

items.q: Most motorcycle turn signals turn off automatically after a turn.

fact: The larger a truck or bus is, the larger its blind spots, the more room it needs to turn, and the longer it takes to stop and to pass.
why: Size and weight limit how quickly a large vehicle can see, stop, and move.

items.q: Large trucks can usually stop in a shorter distance than cars.
Compared to a car, a large truck generally has:

fact: Leave more than 3 seconds of following distance behind a motorcycle, and even more on wet or slick roads.
why: Motorcycles may stop or swerve suddenly for gravel, seams, or other road problems.

items.q: Behind a motorcycle, you should leave MORE than how many seconds of following distance?
You are following a motorcycle on a rainy day. What should you do?
choices: Leave even more than 3 seconds of space
Follow at 1 second so the rider sees you
Keep the same space as on a dry day

fact: Use extra caution around snowplows. The blade throws snow up and off the road, which can cause blizzard-like conditions for drivers following too closely.
why: Following closely puts you in a cloud of snow where you cannot see.

items.q: You are behind a snowplow that is clearing the road. What should you do?
choices: Stay well back because blowing snow can block your view
Follow closely to drive on the cleared road
Pass it right away on the snowy side

items.q: Following close behind a working snowplow is safe because the road behind it is already cleared.

fact: A loaded truck with good brakes needs about 450 feet to stop from 55 mph on a dry road.
why: Heavy vehicles take much longer to stop, so leave them extra space.

items.q: About how many feet does a loaded truck need to stop from 55 mph on a dry road?
About how far does a loaded truck going 55 mph on dry pavement need to stop?

fact: When following a large vehicle, increase your following distance so you can see most of the road ahead.
why: A large vehicle blocks your view of hazards in front of it.

items.q: You are following a large truck and cannot see the road ahead of it. What should you do?
choices: Drop back so you can see more of the road
Move closer so the truck blocks the wind
Drive on the shoulder to see ahead

items.q: A large vehicle ahead of you can block your view of the road, so you should increase your following distance.

fact: If you are behind a large vehicle and cannot see the driver's mirrors, the driver cannot see you. Avoid driving beside large vehicles for long periods.
why: Large vehicles have blind spots behind them and on each side.
hook: Can't see their mirrors? They can't see you.

items.q: You are following a large truck and cannot see its side mirrors. What does this mean?
choices: The truck driver cannot see you
You are at a safe distance
The truck driver can see you clearly

items.q: Large trucks have blind spots behind them and on both sides.

fact: When passing a large vehicle, keep a steady speed. Do not move back in front of it until you can see its cab in your rear-view mirror.
why: Cutting in too soon and slowing down leaves the truck driver no time or room to stop.

items.q: After passing a large truck, when is it safe to move back into its lane?
choices: When you can see the truck's cab in your rear-view mirror
As soon as your back bumper clears its front bumper

items.q: After passing a truck, it is fine to pull in close in front of it and slow down.

fact: Vehicles carrying hazardous materials have placards and must stop at all railroad crossings. Be ready to stop if you are following one.
why: Knowing they must stop keeps you from rear-ending them at a crossing.

items.q: You are following a truck with a hazardous materials placard toward a railroad crossing. What should you expect?
choices: The truck will stop at the crossing
The truck will speed up over the tracks
The truck will turn away from the tracks
Nothing different from any other vehicle

items.q: Vehicles carrying hazardous materials must stop at all railroad crossings.

fact: Pilot vehicles have amber lights and warn of oversized loads. When one comes toward you, slow down and move as far right as you can. If following one, increase your following distance.
why: An oversized load may take up more than its own lane, especially on bridges and curves.

items.q: An oncoming vehicle with amber lights and a sign is leading a very wide load. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and move as far right as possible
Speed up to get past quickly
Move to the center of the road
Stop in your lane and wait

items.q: What color lights do pilot vehicles for large loads use?

fact: Large vehicles may swing left before turning right. Never try to squeeze by on the right side of a large vehicle that is turning right.
why: Squeezing past on the right is a frequent cause of crashes with large vehicles.

items.q: A truck ahead has its right signal on but has moved toward the left lane. There is a gap on its right. What should you do?
choices: Stay back and let it finish the right turn
Drive through the gap on its right
Honk and pass on the right
Pass it on the left quickly

items.q: When a large truck swings left to make a right turn, you may pass it on the right.

fact: Dim your high beams when you are within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 200 feet of a vehicle you are following.
why: High beams can blind other drivers, either directly or through their mirrors.

items.q: Within how many feet of an oncoming vehicle must you dim your high beams?
Within how many feet of a vehicle you are coming up behind must you dim your high beams?
You are driving at night with high beams on and see a car coming toward you. At what distance must you switch to low beams?

fact: At 35 mph, total stopping distance is about 60 to 100 feet on a dry road, 120 feet or more on a wet road, 180 feet or more on packed snow, and 600 feet or more on ice.
why: Less grip between tires and road means brakes take much longer to stop the car.

items.q: According to the handbook chart, about how many feet (or more) does a car going 35 mph need to stop on an icy road?
According to the handbook chart, about how many feet (or more) does a car going 35 mph need to stop on packed snow?
At 35 mph on a dry road, about how far does it take to stop?
At 35 mph, a wet road needs about 120 feet or more to stop.

fact: When you see a large animal such as a deer, elk, or moose on or near the road, slow down and drive carefully, because more of them are usually nearby.
why: These animals travel in herds, so one animal is often a sign that others will follow.

items.q: A deer crosses the road ahead of you and runs into the trees. What should you do next?
choices: Slow down and watch for more deer
Speed up to get past the area quickly
Stop in your lane and wait for an hour

items.q: Why should you slow down after seeing one elk near the road?
choices: Elk always turn around and come back
Idaho law requires you to stop for wildlife

fact: On a narrow mountain road, sound your horn when you come to a curve where you cannot see around it.
why: The horn warns drivers you cannot see who may be coming around the curve toward you.

items.q: You are driving on a narrow mountain road and come to a sharp curve. Rocks block your view of what is around it. What should you do?
choices: Sound your horn as you approach the curve
Move to the center of the road
Speed up to get through the curve
Turn on your high beams in daylight

items.q: On a narrow mountain road, you should sound your horn before a curve where your view is blocked.

fact: When going down a long hill, use a lower gear to control your speed. Never coast downhill in neutral or with the clutch pushed in.
why: A lower gear lets the engine help slow the car, so the brakes do not have to do all the work, and coasting takes away that control.
hook: Low gear going down; never neutral.

items.q: What is the best way to control your speed on a long downhill mountain road?
choices: Press the clutch and use the brakes

items.q: You are driving down a long, steep mountain grade. You want to save fuel. What should you do?
choices: Stay in a lower gear and keep the car in gear
Shift into neutral and let the car coast
Hold the clutch down and ride the brakes
Speed up so you spend less time on the hill

items.q: Using a lower gear on a long downhill helps you control your speed.

fact: On mountain roads, keep your vehicle near the right edge of the road, away from traffic coming toward you.
why: Mountain roads are often narrow and curvy, so staying right gives oncoming vehicles more room.

items.q: Where should you position your vehicle when driving on a mountain road?
choices: Close to the right edge, away from oncoming traffic
Close to the center line for a better view
In the middle of the lane at all times

items.q: On mountain roads, you should drive close to the center line so you can see around curves.

fact: If a small animal is in the road, think of your own safety first. Do not try to swerve around it unless you are sure it is safe.
why: Swerving suddenly can cause you to lose control or hit another vehicle, which is worse than hitting a small animal.

items.q: A rabbit runs into the road in front of you. A car is coming in the other lane. What should you do?
choices: Stay in your lane and do not swerve
Swerve into the other lane to miss it
Swerve onto the shoulder at full speed
Slam on the brakes and turn the wheel sharply

items.q: You should always swerve to avoid a small animal in the road.

fact: In Idaho, horses, cattle, sheep, goats, and other livestock being moved across a road under control have the right-of-way. Be careful and work with the people moving them.
why: Herds are slow and unpredictable, and the people moving them need drivers to wait.

items.q: Who has the right-of-way when ranch workers are moving a herd of cattle across a highway?
You come over a hill and see ranch workers moving sheep across the road. What should you do?
choices: Slow down, wait, and follow the workers' directions
Honk and drive slowly through the herd
Go around the herd on the shoulder
Flash your lights so the workers move the sheep

fact: About 90% of driving choices are based on what you see, and your vision is reduced at night. At night, always drive slowly enough that you can stop within the distance you can see ahead.
why: Your vision is reduced at night, and you need time to react to anything that appears in your headlights.

items.q: How fast should you drive at night?
choices: Slow enough to stop within the distance you can see
The same speed you drive in daylight
Exactly 10 mph under the speed limit
As fast as the car ahead of you

items.q: About what percent of driving choices are based on what you see?

fact: If you hit livestock on open range or being moved under control, the animal's owner does not have to pay for damage to you or your vehicle. If you were careless, you may have to pay for the injured or killed animal.
why: On open range the animals are allowed to be there, so drivers are responsible for watching for them.

items.q: At night on open range, you hit a cow that was standing on the road. Your car is damaged. Who must pay for your car?
choices: The cow's owner is not responsible for your car
The cow's owner must pay for all damage
The county must pay for the damage
The state must pay because it owns the road

items.q: If you hit a cow on open range, the cow's owner must pay for the damage to your vehicle.

fact: Open range is almost all land outside city limits and herd districts where livestock may roam. Fences do not mean animals are absent, so watch for them, especially at night.
why: Animals on open range can be on the road with no warning, and they are hard to see in the dark.

items.q: In Idaho, what does "open range" mean?
choices: Most areas outside city limits where livestock may roam
Only federal land in the mountains
Any road with no speed limit

items.q: Livestock may be on the road in open range even where there are fences.

fact: If an animal moves in front of you too quickly to avoid safely, hitting it may be the safest choice. Focus on keeping control of your vehicle before, during, and after the impact.
why: Losing control by swerving can cause a worse crash than hitting the animal.

items.q: An animal jumps in front of your car and there is no safe way to avoid it. What should you focus on?
choices: Turning sharply into the other lane
Letting go of the steering wheel

items.q: When an animal appears too suddenly to avoid, hitting it can be safer than swerving.

fact: Switch to low beams when you approach an oncoming vehicle, when you follow another vehicle, and on roads that have street lighting.
why: High beams can blind other drivers and are not needed on lighted roads.

items.q: When should you dim your headlights to low beam?
You should keep your high beams on when following another car at night so you can see farther.

fact: At night you can see about 350 feet ahead with high beams and about 100 feet ahead with low beams.
why: Knowing how far you can see helps you choose a speed that lets you stop in time.

items.q: About how many feet ahead can you see at night with your high beams on?
About how many feet ahead can you see at night with your low beams on?
About how far can you see ahead at night using low beams?

fact: Turn on your headlights, not just your parking lights, from sunset to sunrise and any time you cannot see more than 500 feet ahead.
why: Headlights help you see the road and help other drivers see you.

items.q: Headlights are required in the daytime when you cannot see clearly farther than how many feet?
When must you turn on your headlights?
Parking lights alone are enough when driving after sunset.

fact: Do not look into the headlights of oncoming vehicles. Look down toward the lower right side of your lane instead.
why: Looking away keeps the bright light out of your eyes so you are not blinded.

items.q: Where should you look when an oncoming car's headlights are bright?
choices: Toward the lower right side of your lane

items.q: At night, an oncoming car's lights are making it hard to see. What should you do with your eyes?
choices: Shift them down and to the right side of your lane
Stare at the car's lights until it passes

fact: Never wear sunglasses when driving in low light, such as at night or dusk.
why: Your vision is already reduced in low light, and sunglasses make it even harder to see.

items.q: Wearing sunglasses at night helps reduce glare and is a safe habit.
When should you NOT wear sunglasses while driving?
choices: When the road is covered in bright snow

fact: The gray hours of twilight and dawn are the most dangerous times of day to drive.
why: In the gray, low light it is hard to see other vehicles, people, and animals.

items.q: Which times of day are the most dangerous for driving?
Twilight and dawn are among the most dangerous times of day to drive.

fact: It is safest not to drive in fog, dust storms, or heavy rain. If you must, slow down, and if it gets too bad, pull off the road and stop instead of creeping along.
why: A car moving very slowly in low visibility can be hit by drivers who cannot see it.

items.q: You are driving in fog that keeps getting thicker until you can barely see. What should you do?
choices: Pull off the road and stop
Creep along in your lane at 5 mph
Turn on your high beams and keep going
Follow the taillights ahead very closely

items.q: If fog becomes too thick, you should pull off the road and stop.

fact: In fog, smoke, dust, or rain during the day, use your low beam headlights.
why: High beams reflect off fog and dust back into your eyes, while low beams light the road better.

items.q: Which lights work best in fog or dust?
High beams are the best choice when driving in fog.

fact: Do not use cruise control when the road is wet or icy.
why: On a slippery road you need full control of your speed at all times.

items.q: You should not use cruise control on wet or icy roads.
When should you NOT use cruise control?
choices: When the road is wet or icy

fact: Stay two car lengths behind a snowplow for every 10 mph you are driving.
why: Plows spread sand that can damage your car, and the snow they throw makes it hard to see.
hook: 2 car lengths per 10 mph behind a plow.

items.q: How many car lengths should you stay behind a snowplow for every 10 mph of speed?
You are driving 30 mph behind a snowplow. How many car lengths back should you stay?
How far should you stay behind a snowplow truck?
choices: Two car lengths for every 10 mph
One car length for every 10 mph

fact: If you are driving in front of a snowplow, do not brake suddenly. The heavy plow cannot stop as quickly as your car.
why: A heavy truck needs much more distance to stop, so a sudden stop in front of it could cause a crash.

items.q: A snowplow truck can stop as quickly as a car, so it is fine to brake suddenly in front of one.
Why should you avoid braking suddenly in front of a snowplow?
choices: The heavy plow cannot stop as quickly as your car
The plow driver cannot see brake lights
Sudden braking is illegal in winter
The plow will spray sand on your car

fact: Do not pass a snowplow unless you really must. If you pass, do it only when you can clearly see ahead, never on the side where it is spraying snow, and do not pull back in right in front of it.
why: The force of thrown snow can push your car out of control, and plow blades covered in snow are hard to see.

items.q: If you must pass a snowplow, which side should you avoid?
choices: The side where it is spraying snow
Neither side; you may pass on either side
The side away from the spray
No side, as long as you pass quickly

items.q: If you must pass a snowplow, do it only when you can clearly see the road ahead.

fact: If your car starts to hydroplane, keep a steady speed in a straight line and slowly ease off the gas. Do not stop or turn quickly until the tires grip again.
why: Sudden braking or steering while the tires are on water can cause a skid.

items.q: While driving in heavy rain, you feel your car start to float on the water. What should you do?
choices: Slowly take your foot off the gas and keep straight
Speed up to get through the water

items.q: If your car hydroplanes, you should slam on the brakes.

fact: Up to about 35 mph, most tires grip a wet road. At about 55 mph, tires may lose all contact with the road and hydroplane, riding on top of the water.
why: At higher speeds the tires cannot push water out of the way fast enough.

items.q: At about what speed may your tires lose all contact with a wet road?
Up to about what speed do most tires still grip a wet road?
What happens when your car hydroplanes?
choices: You cannot brake, speed up, or steer
The car only pulls to the right

fact: In bad visibility, avoid using your emergency flashers while you are moving.
why: Other drivers may think your car is stopped.

items.q: In fog, you should drive with your emergency flashers on so others can see you.
Why should you avoid using emergency flashers while driving in fog?
choices: Other drivers may think you are stopped

fact: To lower the chance of hydroplaning, slow down in rain, slush, or standing water, replace worn tires, and keep tires properly inflated.
why: Slower speeds and good tires help keep your tires in contact with the road.

items.q: Which helps prevent hydroplaning?
choices: Letting some air out of the tires

items.q: Worn tires make hydroplaning less likely.

fact: Roads are most slippery when a light rain first starts, because oil on the road mixes with water and forms a greasy film. Wet roads can be as dangerous as icy roads.
why: The oily film makes tires lose grip before the rain washes it away.

items.q: When is a road especially slippery during rain?
choices: When a light rain first begins
After it has rained for several hours

items.q: Wet roads can be as dangerous as icy roads.

fact: Bridges, overpasses, and shady spots can be icy when the rest of the road is not. Ice forms sooner and stays longer on bridges and overpasses.
why: Bridges are open to cold air underneath and get no warmth from the ground.

items.q: Where is ice likely to form first on a cold day?
Why do bridges ice over sooner than other roads?
choices: Cold air reaches them from below and they get no ground warmth
They are always in the shade

items.q: Ice can stay on bridges and overpasses after other parts of the road are clear.

fact: On ice or snow, start slowing down at least three times sooner than normal before turning or stopping.
why: Slippery roads greatly increase the distance needed to slow down and stop.

items.q: On snowy or icy roads, you should begin slowing for a stop at least how many times sooner than normal?
On slippery winter roads, which is a key to safety?
choices: Slower speeds and longer following distances
Spinning the tires to get moving
Following closely to use the tracks ahead

fact: Never drive through a flooded road. Turn around and find another route, because a road under water may be washed out.
why: You cannot see how deep the water is or whether the road under it is still there.

items.q: After a thunderstorm, you see water flowing across the road ahead. It does not look very deep. What should you do?
choices: Turn around and find another route
Drive through slowly in low gear
Drive through fast to avoid stalling
Follow another car through the water

items.q: It is safe to drive through a flooded road if the water looks shallow.

fact: If your vehicle stalls in rising flood water, leave it right away and get to higher ground.
why: Quickly rising water can cover the vehicle and sweep it away with you inside.

items.q: Your car stalls in rising flood water. What should you do?
choices: Leave the car right away and move to higher ground
Stay in the car and wait for help
Keep trying to restart the engine
Push the car forward through the water

items.q: If your car stalls in rising flood water, you should leave it and go to higher ground.

fact: Six inches of fast-moving water can knock a person off their feet, and two feet of fast-moving water can wash away a vehicle.
why: Moving water is far more powerful than it looks.
hook: 6 inches knocks you down; 2 feet floats your car.

items.q: How many feet of fast-moving water can wash away a vehicle?
As little as how many inches of fast-moving water can knock you off your feet?
About how deep must fast-moving water be to wash away a vehicle?

fact: If you are stranded and run your engine for heat, make sure the exhaust pipe is clear of snow.
why: A blocked exhaust pipe can push dangerous fumes into the car.

items.q: You are stuck in a snowstorm and want to run the engine to stay warm. What must you check first?
choices: That the exhaust pipe is clear of snow
That the windows are fully closed and sealed

items.q: When stranded in snow, it is safe to run the engine for heat without checking the exhaust pipe.

fact: If you get stranded while heavy snow is falling, stay with your vehicle. Most deaths happen when people leave their car, get lost, and freeze.
why: Your car gives shelter and is easier for rescuers to find than a person on foot.

items.q: Your car gets stuck on a mountain road during heavy snowfall. What is the safest choice?
choices: Walk to find the nearest town
Leave the car and look for a house
Hike to higher ground for a phone signal

items.q: Most winter deaths of stranded drivers happen when they leave the car and get lost.

fact: During hard braking with ABS (anti-lock braking system), a pump motor noise and a pulsing brake pedal are normal. Keep your foot on the pedal. ABS lets you keep steering but does not shorten stopping distance.
why: Drivers who are surprised by the noise may lift their foot, which makes the stop longer.

items.q: You brake hard in an emergency and feel the brake pedal pulsing with a buzzing noise. Your car has ABS (anti-lock braking system). What should you do?
choices: Keep steady pressure on the pedal
Take your foot off the brake
Pump the pedal to stop the pulsing

items.q: Anti-lock brakes make your car stop in a shorter distance.

fact: In an emergency stop with anti-lock brakes (ABS), press the brake pedal firmly and keep steady pressure. Do not pump the brakes.
why: ABS (anti-lock braking system) pumps the brakes for you faster than you can, and pumping yourself makes it work worse and increases stopping distance.
hook: ABS (anti-lock braking system): press hard and hold.

items.q: How should you brake in an emergency if your car has ABS (anti-lock braking system)?
choices: Press firmly and hold steady pressure

items.q: With anti-lock brakes, you should keep steady pressure on the brake pedal in a hard stop.

fact: If your car starts to skid, do not brake. Take your foot off the gas and steer in the direction of the skid. If the rear wheels slide right, turn the front wheels right.
why: Steering the way the back of the car is sliding lines the wheels back up so you can regain control.
hook: Steer where the back end is going.

items.q: On an icy road, the back of your car begins sliding to the right. What should you do?
choices: Take your foot off the gas and steer to the right
Brake hard and hold the wheel straight

items.q: What is the first thing to do with your feet when a skid starts?
choices: Take your foot off the gas pedal
Press the clutch and brake together

items.q: In a skid, you should steer in the direction the rear wheels are sliding.

fact: If your car breaks down, pull completely off the road if you can, turn on your emergency flashers, and raise the hood. If you cannot get off the road, do not stop just over a hill or around a curve.
why: Many crashes happen because drivers do not see a stalled vehicle in time.

items.q: Your car stalls on the highway and you pull onto the shoulder. What signals to others that you need help?
If you cannot get off the road, stopping just past the top of a hill is a good choice.

fact: If your car breaks down and you have flares, place them 200 to 300 feet behind your car. If you have no flares, stand off the road and wave traffic around, using a white cloth if you have one.
why: Flares give approaching drivers time to see the problem and move over.

items.q: How far behind your stalled car should you place emergency flares?
What is the minimum distance, in feet, behind your stalled car to place flares?

fact: Without ABS (anti-lock braking system), brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels. If the wheels lock and the car skids, quickly ease off the brake, then press again, repeating until you stop.
why: Locked wheels slide and cannot steer, so releasing lets them roll and grip again.

items.q: Your car does not have ABS (anti-lock braking system). During a hard stop, you feel the wheels lock and the car start to skid. What should you do?
choices: Quickly let up on the brake, then press again

items.q: Without ABS (anti-lock braking system), how hard should you press the brake in a quick stop?
choices: As hard as you can without locking the wheels
As hard as possible, even if the wheels lock
Very lightly so you never skid

fact: To avoid a crash you can steer or change speed. If you cannot stop in time, try to steer out of the way, and stay off the brakes while turning if possible.
why: You have more steering control when the brakes are not being applied.

items.q: A car suddenly stops ahead and you know you cannot stop in time. There is an open lane beside you. What is the best choice?
choices: Steer into the open lane, staying off the brakes while turning
Brake as hard as possible while turning sharply
Speed up and hit the car

items.q: When steering to avoid a crash, you have more control if you stay off the brakes while turning.

fact: If you are about to be hit from the rear, press your head against the headrest. If hit from the side, be ready to steer. If hit from the front while wearing a seat belt, protect your face with your arms and hands.
why: Each position lowers injury from the direction of impact.

items.q: You see in your mirror that a car is about to hit you from behind. What should you do?
choices: Press the back of your head against the headrest
Turn around to look at the car
Lean forward toward the steering wheel

items.q: What is the best protection in any crash?
choices: Buckling your seat belt before the trip
Bracing your hands on the dashboard
Sitting close to the steering wheel

fact: If a car is coming at you in your lane, slow down, flash your lights, honk, and move as far right as you can. Never swerve left. If you cannot avoid a crash, steer so you hit at an angle, not head-on.
why: The other driver may correct back into their own lane and hit you from the side if you go left.
hook: Head-on threat: go right, never left.

items.q: A car is coming toward you in your lane on a two-lane road. What should you do?
choices: Slow down, honk, and move as far right as possible
Stop in the middle of your lane
Speed up to get past quickly

items.q: If a car is coming at you in your lane, you should swerve left into the other lane.

fact: If you hit an unattended vehicle or other property, make a reasonable effort to find the owner. If you cannot, leave a note with your name, phone number, and what happened.
why: The owner has a right to know who damaged their property.

items.q: You back into a parked car in a lot and dent it. No one is around. What must you do?
choices: Try to find the owner, and if you cannot, leave a note with your name and phone number
Drive away since no one saw it
Wait one minute and then leave
Leave a note with only your license plate number

items.q: If you hit a parked car and cannot find the owner, you may leave without doing anything.

fact: If you come to a crash and police or medical help are already there, do not stop; follow the officers' directions. If you are the first to arrive, stop, call 911, and help if you can.
why: Extra stopped cars can block emergency workers, but the first person there may be needed.

items.q: You drive past a crash where police and an ambulance are already working. What should you do?
choices: Keep moving as the officers direct

fact: Idaho is part of the Driver License Compact. If an Idaho driver is convicted of a traffic offense in another state, it goes on the Idaho record and is treated as if it happened in Idaho.
why: Member states share records so drivers cannot escape penalties by breaking laws away from home.

items.q: You have an Idaho license and get convicted of speeding while visiting another member state. What happens?
choices: It is added to your Idaho driving record
It stays only on that other state's records
It is ignored because you are not a resident there
It is removed after you return to Idaho

items.q: Under the Driver License Compact, only serious offenses like DUI (driving under the influence) are reported to your home state, not minor moving violations.

fact: Idaho keeps a driving record for you even if you have never been issued a license. Your driving privileges can be suspended, canceled, or revoked before you ever get a license.
why: Breaking traffic laws is dangerous whether or not you hold a license, so the state tracks it either way.

items.q: Your driving privileges can be suspended even if you have never been issued a driver's license.
Who does the Idaho Transportation Department keep a driving record for?
choices: Drivers with and without a license
Only drivers with a full license
Only drivers with a crash on record

fact: Driving courses only remove points from your record. The conviction itself stays on your record.
why: The course lowers your point total, but it does not erase the fact that you broke the law.

items.q: After you finish a Defensive Driving Course, the conviction still stays on your driving record.
What does an approved driving course remove from your record?

fact: Finishing an ITD-approved Defensive Driving Course removes up to 3 points. Points can be removed this way only once every 3 years, and the points must already be on your record before you finish the course.
why: The course rewards drivers who work to improve, but limits it so it cannot be used again and again.

items.q: What is the most points an ITD-approved Defensive Driving Course can remove?
Points may be removed by a course once every how many years?
When must points be on your record to be removed by a Defensive Driving Course?

fact: If you get 12 to 17 points in any 12 months, your license may be suspended for 30 days.
why: Many violations in a short time show a pattern of unsafe driving.

items.q: How many points in any 12 months can lead to a 30-day suspension (lowest number)?
How long is the suspension for 12 to 17 points in 12 months?
In the last 12 months you have collected 14 points. What penalty may you face?

fact: If you get 24 or more points in any 36 months, your license may be suspended for 6 months.
why: This is the longest point suspension because it is for drivers with the most violations.

items.q: How many points in any 36 months can lead to a 6-month suspension (lowest number)?
How many months long is the suspension for 24 or more points in 36 months?
What penalty may follow 24 or more points in any 36 months?

fact: If you get 18 to 23 points in any 24 months, your license may be suspended for 90 days.
why: The more points you collect, the longer the state removes you from the road.

items.q: Within how many months must 18 to 23 points be collected to lead to a 90-day suspension?
How long is the suspension for 18 to 23 points in 24 months?
What penalty may follow 18 to 23 points in any 24 months?

fact: Idaho uses a point system. Each moving traffic violation on your record adds 1 to 4 points.
why: Points let the state track drivers who keep breaking traffic laws and act before they cause a crash.

items.q: What is the most points a single moving violation can add to your Idaho driving record?
How many points does one moving traffic violation add to your record in Idaho?

fact: If you get 8 to 11 points in any 12 months, the department may send you a warning letter.
why: A warning gives you a chance to change your driving before a suspension.

items.q: What is the lowest number of points in 12 months that can earn you a warning letter?
What action may the department take if you collect 8 to 11 points in 12 months?

fact: A Traffic Safety Education Course can remove up to 4 points. It must be offered by the officer and accepted at the time of the ticket, and you must finish it within 45 days of the citation.
why: The course is a quick chance to learn from a mistake right after it happens.

items.q: Within how many days of the citation must you finish a Traffic Safety Education Course?
What is the most points a Traffic Safety Education Course can remove?
When must a Traffic Safety Education Course be offered and accepted?
choices: At the time of the citation

fact: Your license can be suspended or revoked for things like DUI (driving under the influence), reckless driving, fleeing a police officer, leaving the scene of a crash, refusing or failing an evidentiary test, and not carrying vehicle insurance.
why: These actions put other people in serious danger or avoid responsibility for harm.

items.q: Which of these can lead to the loss of your driving privileges in Idaho?
choices: Driving a car older than 20 years
Driving at night with a full license

items.q: Leaving the scene of a crash that only damaged property cannot lead to a suspension.

fact: Failing to attend school or meet school requirements is one reason your license can be suspended. So is breaking a license restriction, such as daylight-only or corrective lenses.
why: Driving is a privilege that comes with responsibilities beyond the road itself.

items.q: Not attending school can be a reason for losing your driving privileges in Idaho.
Your license says you must wear corrective lenses, but you drive without them. What could happen?
choices: Nothing, if you can still see the road
You only get a warning letter by law
You must retake the vision test only

fact: GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalty suspensions are absolute: no driving of any kind is allowed. They are added on top of any permit cancellation or other suspension from a court or the department.
why: The penalty is meant to fully stop a young driver from driving for the whole period.

items.q: During a GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalty suspension, you may not drive at all, not even to school or work.
During a GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalty suspension, what driving is allowed?

fact: Drivers under 17 get a warning letter for their first moving violation conviction.
why: Young drivers get one warning so they can correct their habits before losing driving privileges.

items.q: GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalties apply to all drivers under what age?
You are 16 and convicted of your first moving violation. What GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalty applies?

fact: Drivers under 17 lose their driving privileges for 30 days after a second moving violation conviction.
why: A second violation shows the warning did not work, so a real penalty follows.

items.q: How many days is the GDL (Graduated Driver's License) suspension for a second moving violation conviction for a driver under 17?
You are 16 and just got your second moving violation conviction. What is the GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalty?

fact: Drivers under 17 lose their driving privileges for 60 days after a third or later moving violation conviction.
why: Penalties grow with each violation to stop a pattern of unsafe driving.

items.q: How many days is the GDL (Graduated Driver's License) suspension for a third moving violation conviction for a driver under 17?
For a driver under 17, a third moving violation conviction leads to a 90-day suspension.
You are 16 and were just convicted of your third moving violation. What GDL (Graduated Driver's License) penalty applies?

fact: If your license is suspended, you may qualify for a restricted permit to drive to places like work or medical treatment. If the department suspended you, apply to ITD (Idaho Transportation Department) in Boise; if a court suspended you, apply to that court.
why: A restricted permit lets people meet basic needs while still limiting their driving.

items.q: A court suspended your license after a conviction. Where do you ask for restricted driving privileges?
choices: Any county DMV (Division of Motor Vehicles) office

items.q: A restricted driving permit lets you drive anywhere you want during a suspension.

fact: If you break Idaho's no-insurance law, you must show proof of financial responsibility for 1 year for a first offense, or 3 years for a second offense within 5 years.
why: Uninsured drivers leave crash victims without a way to pay for damages.

items.q: For a first no-insurance offense, for how many years must you show proof of financial responsibility?
For a second no-insurance offense within 5 years, for how many years must you show proof of financial responsibility?
You are caught driving without insurance for the first time. How long must you show proof of financial responsibility?

fact: To get your license back after a suspension for serious offenses like DUI (driving under the influence) or reckless driving, you must pay a reinstatement fee and show proof of financial responsibility (an SR-22 insurance certificate) for 3 years.
why: Drivers who committed serious offenses must prove they are insured in case they cause harm again.

items.q: For how many years must you show proof of financial responsibility after a DUI (driving under the influence) or reckless driving suspension?
What is the accepted proof of financial responsibility after a serious offense?
choices: An SR-22 certificate from your insurer
A copy of your vehicle title

fact: Every vehicle must have two brake systems. At 20 mph on dry pavement, the foot brake must stop the vehicle within 25 feet, and the parking brake within 55 feet.
why: A second brake system lets you stop if the first one fails.

items.q: Within how many feet must foot brakes stop a vehicle going 20 mph on dry pavement?
Within how many feet must the parking (emergency) brake stop a vehicle going 20 mph on dry pavement?
Why must every vehicle have two brake systems?
choices: So one still works if the other fails
So the car can stop twice as fast
So the passenger can also brake
So the brakes wear out more slowly

fact: Vehicles need two headlights with high and low beams. High beams must let you see people and vehicles at least 350 feet ahead; low beams must light the road at least 100 feet ahead.
why: You need to see far enough ahead at night to react to hazards in time.

items.q: How must headlights be aimed?
choices: To light the road without blinding oncoming drivers
As high as possible to see farther

items.q: High beams must let you see people and vehicles at least how many feet away?
Low beams must light the road at least how many feet ahead?
It is illegal to cover your headlights with material that light cannot pass through.

fact: You may not drive a vehicle that is mechanically unsafe. Idaho has no yearly safety inspection, but an officer who finds your vehicle unsafe or missing required equipment can give you a citation.
why: The driver is responsible for keeping the vehicle safe for everyone on the road.

items.q: Even without an annual safety inspection, an officer can cite you for an unsafe vehicle.
Who is responsible for fixing a vehicle that lacks vital equipment?

fact: Every motor vehicle must have working red or amber brake lights that come on when you press the foot brake. They must be visible from at least 100 feet behind in normal sunlight.
why: Drivers behind you need a clear warning that you are slowing or stopping.

items.q: Brake lights must be visible from at least how many feet behind the vehicle in normal sunlight?
What colors may brake lights be?
Brake lights must turn on when you press the foot brake.

fact: Every motor vehicle must have a horn that can be heard at least 200 feet away. Horns that are unreasonably loud or harsh are not allowed.
why: A horn must be loud enough to warn others but not so harsh that it startles or disturbs people.

items.q: Which horn meets Idaho law?
choices: One heard at 200 feet that is not harsh
An extra-loud air horn on a small car
A horn that plays music loudly

items.q: A vehicle's horn must be heard from at least how many feet away?
Any horn is legal in Idaho, no matter how loud or harsh it sounds.

fact: Most motor vehicles and trailers must have at least two red taillights, one on the left rear and one on the right rear, visible from 500 feet behind. Motorcycles and vehicles built before 1956 need at least one.
why: Taillights let drivers behind you see your vehicle from far away in the dark.

items.q: Taillights on a modern car must be visible from at least how many feet behind?
How many red taillights must a modern passenger car have, at minimum?

fact: Each tire should have at least 2/32 of an inch of tread.
why: Worn tires lose grip, especially on wet or icy roads.

items.q: What is the minimum tire tread depth listed in the Idaho handbook?
Each tire should have at least how many 32nds of an inch of tread?

fact: Vehicles must have a rearview mirror that shows at least 200 feet of road behind. If a load or trailer blocks the rear view, the vehicle needs a mirror on each side.
why: You must always be able to see traffic behind you.

items.q: A rearview mirror must give a view of at least how many feet of highway behind you?
You are towing a trailer that blocks the view through your rear window. What mirrors does your vehicle need?
choices: One mirror on each side of the vehicle
One mirror on the driver's side only
No mirrors are needed if you drive slowly

fact: Windows and windshields must be safety glass, kept free of stickers not required by law, not blocked by hanging objects, and cleared of frost, snow, and dirt before you drive.
why: Anything that blocks your view can hide a hazard until it is too late.

items.q: On a cold morning your windshield is covered in frost except for a small spot. What should you do?
choices: Clear all the frost from the windows before driving
Drive slowly and look through the clear spot
Drive with the window down to see
Wait until the defroster clears it while driving

items.q: You may put any stickers you like on your windshield as long as they are small.

fact: Safety experts recommend that all children under 13 ride in the back seat, and a rear-facing car seat should never be placed in front of an active passenger air bag.
why: A front air bag opens with great force and can seriously hurt a child.

items.q: You are driving your 11-year-old cousin. Where is the safest place for them to sit?
choices: In the front seat with the air bag on
In the front seat with the seat moved forward

items.q: Children younger than what age should ride in the back seat, according to the safety recommendation?
A rear-facing car seat is safest in the front seat in front of the air bag.

fact: Idaho law requires children 6 years old or younger to be properly secured in approved child safety seats, used on every trip.
why: Adult seat belts do not fit small children, and most child crash deaths and injuries can be prevented with proper seats.
hook: 6 and under = car seat, every trip.

items.q: Children of what age or younger must ride in an approved child safety seat in Idaho?
You are driving your 5-year-old neighbor two blocks to school. What does Idaho law require?
choices: The child must be in an approved safety seat
A regular seat belt is enough for short trips
The child may sit on an adult's lap
No restraint is needed under 25 mph

items.q: A child safety seat is only required on highway trips, not short trips in town.

fact: Idaho law requires every person in a vehicle to wear a seat belt or shoulder strap if the vehicle came from the factory with them.
why: Seat belts greatly lower the chance of serious injury or death and help the driver stay in control.

items.q: Who must wear a seat belt in a vehicle that has factory seat belts?
In Idaho, back-seat passengers must also wear seat belts if the vehicle has them.

fact: Regular vehicles may not have red or blue emergency lights or sirens, bells, or whistles. Those are only for emergency vehicles.
why: Other drivers must be able to trust that red and blue lights and sirens mean a real emergency vehicle.

items.q: Red and blue emergency lights are allowed only on emergency vehicles.
Which equipment is not allowed on a regular passenger car?

fact: Wearing a seat belt cuts your chance of serious injury in a crash by about 50%. Seat belts also help drivers keep control on winding or rough roads or when swerving.
why: A belt holds you in place so you are not thrown around and can keep steering.

items.q: By about what percent do seat belts reduce your chance of serious injury in a crash?
Besides preventing injury, how do seat belts help the driver?
choices: They help you keep control of the car
They make the car use less fuel
They let you drive faster on curves
They make the air bags unnecessary

fact: Studded snow tires may be used only from October 1 to April 30. ITD (Idaho Transportation Department) sometimes changes these dates because of the weather.
why: Studs help on ice but damage dry pavement, so they are limited to the snowy months.

items.q: During what period may studded snow tires normally be used in Idaho?
It is June 15 and your car still has studded snow tires. What is true?
choices: Studded tires are not allowed at this time of year
They are fine if the roads are wet
They are fine all year in Idaho
They are only illegal on freeways

items.q: In Idaho, studded snow tires may be used all year long.

fact: A load must not stick out past the fenders on the left side of the vehicle. On the right side, it may stick out no more than 6 inches past the fenders.
why: A load that sticks out to the left can hit oncoming traffic, so the limit is strict on that side.

items.q: How many inches past the right-side fenders may a load stick out, at most?
You are carrying a long ladder on your car. It sticks out 4 inches past the fenders on the left side. Is this allowed?
choices: No, a load may not extend past the left fenders
Yes, up to 6 inches is allowed on either side
Yes, if a red flag is tied to it

fact: If a load sticks out 4 feet or more past the back of a vehicle, a red flag at least 18 inches square must be on the end. At night, use a red light visible from at least 500 feet instead.
why: Drivers behind you need a clear warning so they do not hit the load.

items.q: A load extending how many feet or more past the rear of a vehicle needs a red flag?
What is the minimum size, in inches square, of the red flag on an overhanging load?
At night you carry lumber that sticks out 5 feet past your truck's tailgate. What must be on the end of the load?
choices: A red light visible from 500 feet
